standfirst: Deltaretrovirus holds two lineages in one module: the primate T-lymphotropic viruses, 678 genomes, and bovine leukaemia virus, 473. They are together because the project's partitioning rule says they should be, and all three of its clauses were measured rather than assumed — same gag-pro-pol-env layout plus tax and rex, peripheral proteins that return no blastp hit across the lineages at e≤1e-3, and one shared splice mechanism claimed under no competing key.

modules.Deltaretrovirus: TAX takes a profile and is not a spliced feature, which corrects the planning for this module. Its first coding exon is 4 nt — the initiator methionine and one base — so about 99.7% of the protein sits in one genomic block and the collinearity triage calls it collinear on 851 deposits. REX is the opposite: a ~60 nt first exon is roughly 12% of a ~170 aa protein, which is what drops it below the collinearity floor. Rex is also not one protein across the module — 156 aa in bovine leukaemia virus, 189 in PTLV-1, 182 in PTLV-3, 170 in HTLV-2 and HTLV-4 — so it is built from one query per lineage and then de-duplicated to one reference per genome.

gaps: The lineage-specific accessories call on 15–30% of exemplars and that is the denominator, not a gap: AS1, G4 and R3 exist only in bovine leukaemia virus and HBZ, p12, p13 and p30 only in the primate lineage, so each can fire on at most its own half of the exemplar set. Three things are genuinely open. Rex references cover the two lineages unevenly — 466 over 473 bovine genomes against 123 over 678 primate ones — because a 20-residue first exon is below what tblastn will report for a query 85% identical to the subject, and a genome with no near reference can be miscalled: HTLV-1 11908.2880 has its rex spliced from inside gag. The single bat deltaretrovirus genome builds no Rex reference at all. And p13 is 100% identical to residues 155–241 of p30 in all seven collection members, so the two cannot be separated by profile alone; 8 of 10 p13 calls are nonetheless the correct 87 aa.
